name: Carhartt-Seo Ironwall Chore Coat
description:
A descendant of the classic duck-canvas chore coat, the Ironwall is built for Tier 2 workers who need something that can take genuine punishment. The fabric is a heavyweight synthetic-cotton duck in faded khaki or engine-room brown, triple-stitched at every seam and bartacked at the stress points. Four patch pockets sit on the front, deep enough to lose a wrench in. The collar is corduroy-lined — a detail borrowed from old American workwear that Carhartt-Seo has never bothered to remove because it works. After a few months of hard use it softens and creases in ways that make it look like it belongs to the person wearing it.

Most of the people who wear this work in fabrication yards, the lower transit corridors, or warehouse logistics. It's not a fashion item and it doesn't try to be. On the Shelf it gets handed down. In Tier 2 neighborhoods it's the default for anyone who works outside or in unregulated spaces. A few Tier 3 people buy it deliberately, either because they grew up in it or because they like the message it sends.
what_it_says: You work with your hands and you don't apologize for it.
worn_by: Shelf survivors who found steady work
story_hooks: A coat found in a locker at an abandoned fabrication yard still has a name tag stitched inside — someone who disappeared six months ago during a corponation site dispute.
A union organizer uses the coat as an identifier; members know to approach anyone wearing a Ironwall with a specific patch on the left shoulder.
The coat's deep pockets are where a Tier 2 courier has been hiding data chips for a client they've never met.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian work jacket with a boxy, purposeful silhouette. Structured and confident without attempting style—the kind of garment that announces competence and durability at a glance. Sits somewhere between heritage Americana and post-industrial pragmatism.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and roomy through the torso and shoulders, designed for layering over thermals or light augmentation rigs. Sleeves are straight and unfitted. Overall impression is that it could swallow you or fit perfectly depending on your frame—it simply doesn't care.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavyweight synthetic-cotton duck blend; the texture of real canvas but engineered for thermal regulation and resistance to industrial solvents. Fades to soft gray-khaki or rust-brown with age.
physical_description.texture: Coarse and honest when new; gradually softens and creases into deep furrows that map the wearer's movements. Seams are visibly thick and proud. The corduroy collar lining is warm and slightly fuzzy against skin.
physical_description.color_scheme: Faded khaki or engine-room brown as primary; natural weathering creates uneven tone variation. Contrast stitching in off-white or cream stands out against the base color, especially at bartacks.
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty snap buttons down the front—brass or brass-look fasteners that age to a dull patina. Four large exterior patch pockets with snap flaps.
distinctive_features: Corduroy-lined collar—a heritage detail that refuses obsolescence
Heavy bartacking at stress points (shoulders, pocket corners, armholes)
Four deep patch pockets positioned for function, not form
Worn hems and collar edges that fray slightly and then stabilize
Subtle Carhartt-Seo branding on the inside back neck or lower pocket
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2 functional—expensive enough to signal serious work, affordable enough to be disposable if truly destroyed. Occasionally worn aspirationally by Tier 3 people.
physical_description.cultural_context: Fabrication yards, warehouse logistics, lower transit corridors, unregulated industrial spaces. Signals someone who works with their hands and their environment—reliable, unkempt by choice, no pretense.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and creased after months of wear; fabric softens and darkens from sweat and handling. Minor oil stains, frayed hems, faded seams. Looks better after two years than it did at purchase.
